The Battle for the Quiet Room

Libraries are adding silent reading rooms again. Can they stay quiet in a loud age?

A group of neatly dressed readers gathered in the reading room this summer to observe a ritual that had nearly disappeared. A group of neatly dressed readers gathered in the reading room this summer to observe a ritual that had nearly disappeared.

Every Thursday evening, a dozen people gather in the back room of a small public library to read. Nobody brings a phone to the table. They bring essays, printed at home or at the library desk, stapled at the corner, and a pencil.

The habit began as an experiment by two librarians who noticed that the most requested service at the counter was no longer borrowing books but printing long articles. People wanted the essays they had bookmarked for months in a form they could finish.

What started as a printing queue became a reading group, then a habit that spread to three other branches. The rules are simple: one essay, read in silence for forty minutes, then twenty minutes of talk.

Retired schoolteachers were the first regulars. They brought red pens, and the habit of writing in the margins. Younger readers followed, some of them surprised at how much they remembered of a piece they had read on paper.
